beats.trigger: ## Getting Going
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: With the right guardrails, you create output that's genuinely yours, not generic.
beats.got: The point is getting AI output that sounds like me and not like everyone else.

beats.trigger: Connect your calendar (M365 / Google Workspace / screenshot fallback) and save a 5-line summary of this week's meetings.
beats.got: Homework involves a snake game and giving the tool my calendar. I wonder what our DPO would say about the calendar part.

beats.trigger: **Package** the guardrails as reusable rules
beats.got: Reusable rules is the only item that sounds like something that could spread beyond me.

beats.trigger: where did LLM output on your own work come out generic, and what made it feel like yours?
beats.got: A fair question about my own work. I can think of HR texts that came out bland.

beats.trigger: The same question. Two answers. What makes the difference?
beats.got: A teaser: the same question gets different answers for some reason.

beats.trigger: Finnish: salmon, rye bread.
beats.got: What I asked earlier in the conversation changed the dinner answer. That is a neat, concrete way to see it.

beats.trigger: Your first prompt and its answer are part of the input to the second prompt.
beats.got: The tool re-reads everything said so far each time. This explains why my chats drift.

beats.trigger: You told the LLM who you are.
beats.got: Telling it my role changes what it suggests, so I can steer it with a sentence about myself.

beats.trigger: Tools, goals, checks, boundaries, and loops come later and depend on it.
beats.got: Several words I do not know yet appear in one list, and I would have liked them explained first.

beats.trigger: You write it once, and it shapes every answer.
beats.got: A file the agent reads at the start of every session. A team could share one, and I would like to know who owns it.

beats.trigger: Change the context, watch the agent's output shift, then package what you learned for the next session.
beats.got: Forty-five minutes building a site about myself, and the real aim is learning to package the learning.

beats.trigger: The mess is the point.
beats.got: I paste in my messy LinkedIn page and get a generic site, so I can compare later versions with it.

beats.trigger: A colleague who lands on it should think *"this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at,"*
beats.got: The site should invite colleagues, not sell to them. I like that, it is how a people leader should show up.

beats.trigger: *"Apply X to Y, but tune for Z."*
beats.got: I can name a framework the model already knows and adjust it. I could do that with frameworks from HR.

beats.trigger: Answer each in your own words, briefly; don't polish.
beats.got: The agent interviews me one beat at a time and then rewrites the page. That is easy to follow.

beats.trigger: Your strengths shape how the whole site sounds.
beats.got: I give it three to five strengths and it regenerates the site.

beats.trigger: Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall for five minutes on what they're great at.
beats.got: It is easier to say what I am against, and that can define what I am for. That is true of me.

beats.trigger: Vague input drifts back to the statistical-default you.
beats.got: Specific complaints work better than categories. I have plenty of those, so this is fun.

beats.trigger: LLMs go easy on their own output.
beats.got: The agent is too kind about its own work, so I should be wary when it grades itself.

beats.trigger: *"Make it look like Stripe's design language"*
beats.got: I can steal a look by naming a famous site. I tried a few and it felt playful.

beats.trigger: so a fresh agent can repeat it on someone else's bio without you re-explaining.
beats.got: The learning ends up in a file another person or agent could use. I see how this travels to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.
beats.got: Every phase added specific context, and that is what made the output mine.

beats.trigger: The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. You got better at feeding it the context that produces YOUR output.
beats.got: The skill is mine, not the model's. It would apply to role descriptions or policies, though the page says nothing about people.

beats.trigger: ## Iterate and Learn
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The move: change something, notice what shifted, adjust, build again.
beats.got: A loop of change, notice, adjust. It is a learning habit rather than a tool trick.

beats.trigger: Agreeable answers won the round the model was tuned on.
beats.got: The model is trained to please, so its self-review flatters. I should not treat it as a verdict.

beats.trigger: Where it doesn't, yours counts.
beats.got: I was there, so my memory of the work outranks the agent's report when they differ.

beats.trigger: Only you could catch a wrong line about you, which is why your own profile is the place to start.
beats.got: Human judgement is what makes the output right. That is the first line in the whole module about people.

beats.trigger: Nobody knows where agents are going, not Anthropic, not your board.
beats.got: Nobody knows the future, so I should experiment. That fits me, though I still want the headcount question answered.

beats.trigger: Expect the generation rules to change a lot. The first pass is rarely right.
beats.got: The agent reviews my rules file against what we actually did, and the first draft will be wrong.

beats.trigger: **compound interest on a rule file.**
beats.got: A rules file gets better each time I redo and reflect. That is a habit I could teach a team.

beats.trigger: Your gut on what is uniquely you carries more weight than the agent's.
beats.got: A second reader that has only the site can test it, but I still trust my own gut more.

beats.trigger: Your domain expertise is the test.
beats.got: Guardrails are structured context, my expertise is the test, and specific context gives specific output.

beats.trigger: Bring a live challenge and working access to Confluence and OneDrive.
beats.got: More homework, and I will need access sorted with IT.

beats.trigger: Karpathy's LLM Wiki post; Lindenberg's memory-architecture piece, optional.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Arrive with enough real material that the memory starts from your world, not generic output.
beats.got: Next time we work on real history, meaning my actual meetings and notes.

beats.trigger: If stuck, scan your next two weeks of calendar; the biggest unresolved item is usually your challenge.
beats.got: I should pick a real open problem. Mine is how roles and hiring change.

beats.trigger: If a connector needs admin approval, tell the training coordinator and keep going.
beats.got: Connecting the agent to company documents needs approval, and I do not want to touch employee data before the works council and DPO know.

beats.trigger: Before it writes anything, ask it for a plan and approve or revise it first.
beats.got: I can ask the agent for a plan and approve it before it edits files. That feels like the right control.

beats.trigger: If a line is blank, name a fallback; do not fill it with a plausible answer.
beats.got: A three-line note with my challenge, my source and my planning control. A blank line needs a named fallback.

beats.trigger: a useful system is a living pile of text the agent can read, maintain, and improve.
beats.got: The memory will be plain text files the agent reads and rewrites.

beats.trigger: The output now travels with a file the agent re-reads next time.
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: What I tell the agent up front, my role, my specifics, what I hate, steers everything after it. A sentence about me changes the answer.
A rules file the agent reads every session is how a habit could spread from me to my HR partners, and I should review it myself because the agent flatters its own work.
My own expertise is the test. The agent drafts and I decide.

monday.move: Write a short rules file for how our HR texts should sound, such as role descriptions, and try it on one real draft.
monday.who: Me, then one HR business partner to review it
monday.stop_condition: The draft needs only light edits, or the file starts to need real employee data.
monday.blocker: Anything with employee data needs the works council and the DPO first, and I have not asked them yet.

misconception.why: The module never touched roles or headcount, so I still expect agents to replace headcount first. The line about human judgement being the test is the nearest thing to a counterweight.

one_line: Good hands-on lesson in how context changes what the AI gives you, but nobody said a word about what it means for our people.
